description: We are a passionate and enthusiastic team of aspiring innovators interested in science, technology, engineering, and space exploration. Our goal is to collaborate, think creatively, and develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges using NASA's open data. We welcome individuals from diverse backgrounds with interests in coding, electronics, research, data analysis, design, and problem-solving.
summary:
Perigee is an interactive Space Mission Design Game that lets players design, launch and manage a complete space mission. Players pick a science goal (Earth observation, weather, the Moon or Mars), choose an orbit and rocket, build the spacecraft, select instruments and plan communications. Six live meters (mass, power, budget, data, communications and time) show how every decision affects the others, and a month-by-month flight simulation with random events decides whether the mission succeeds.
It addresses the challenge by turning separate space topics into one connected system, with solo play or teams of up to four, each taking a role and negotiating trade-offs. Every flight ends with a score out of 100 and a plain-language explanation of why it worked or failed.
This matters because real missions succeed through engineering trade-offs and teamwork, which are hard to learn from theory. Perigee gives students and aspiring engineers a safe place to experiment, fail and learn how missions are designed.
details:
What it does and how it works

Perigee is a game where you plan a space mission and then see if it works. You start by picking a mission, like watching crops from orbit, tracking storms, or searching for water on the Moon. Then you build everything yourself: the orbit, the rocket, the spacecraft, the instruments, and how the data gets back to Earth.

The tricky part is that every choice affects something else. If you add an instrument, the spacecraft gets heavier, needs more power, costs more and produces more data. Six meters on the screen (mass, power, budget, data, communications and time) show this as you go, and a design review points out problems before you launch. When you’re ready, you launch, and the game runs the mission month by month. Things can go wrong, like solar storms or equipment failures. At the end you get a score out of 100 and an explanation of why it worked or didn’t.

You can play alone, or with up to three friends. Each person takes a role and everyone works on the same mission at the same time.

Benefits and impact

Most people learn about orbits, rockets and spacecraft as separate topics. Perigee puts them together, so you can see why engineers have to compromise. You don’t need any space knowledge to start, because the game explains things in simple words as you play. We hope it makes space engineering feel less scary and more fun, and helps students understand how real mission teams think and work together.

Tools we used

We built it as a single web page using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and SVG graphics, so it runs in any browser. Team play uses a real-time room feature, and we tested the game with Node.js. We made the presentation images with Python. All you need to run it is an ordinary computer.

What makes it creative

The spacecraft and the orbit are drawn live as you design, so you can actually see your choices. The scoring rewards good judgment, not just luck: carrying too little spare margin is risky, but carrying too much is wasteful. In team mode, each person controls a different part, so you have to talk and agree on trade-offs. There’s also never just one right answer, since different designs can reach the same goal.

What we thought about

We kept the science simple on purpose, so the numbers teach the idea instead of being exact. We wanted beginners to feel comfortable, so we added easy difficulty levels and a starter design. We tested the game with good and bad designs to make sure the results made sense. We also based the missions on real NASA and ESA work, and we made sure it works without any sign-up, with saved designs staying on your own device.
